_comment: Hand-written introductions for the curated affix pages (each at least 150 words). Every word in <code> must be in the visible ENABLE list; the build checks this. Counts and other examples on the page are computed at build time.

affixes.html:
The prefix un does two different jobs in English, and it helps to keep them apart. Added to an adjective or participle it means “not”: unhappy, unkind, unseen. Added to a verb it reverses an action that was done earlier: you untie a knot you tied and unlock a door you locked. Because both kinds are so productive, word lists contain long runs of un- words that are easy to overlook.

For word games that matters in two ways. First, many long words are simply a shorter word with un in front, so spotting a base word on your rack plus a spare U and N can turn a modest play into a long one. Second, not every word that begins with these two letters is an un- word at all: under, uncle and unit start with the same letters but carry no prefix. The figures below count every word in the list that starts with U-N, whatever its history, and the observations show how many of them still leave a word when the two letters are removed.

The prefix re usually means “again” (reread, rebuild, reheat) or “back” (repay, return). It attaches to a huge number of verbs, which is why the list of words starting with R-E is one of the longest two-letter starts in the whole word list and has to be split into smaller pages here.

Many words that start with these letters have no living prefix, though. In record, regal or reason the opening letters are just part of the word. A quick test is to cover the first two letters: if what remains is a word with a related meaning, the prefix is probably real. The “still form a word” figure below applies a strict spelling version of that test, so it also catches accidental cases such as a word that happens to contain a shorter, unrelated word.

In tile games, a spare R and E are among the most flexible letters to hold, and re- extensions are a common way to lengthen a word already on the board, though only where your game's dictionary accepts the longer form.

The prefix pre comes from Latin and means “before”, either in time or in position. You see the time sense in preview, prepay and preheat, and the position sense in words such as prefix itself, which is a piece fixed before a word. Modern English keeps making new pre- words, so word lists include plenty of fairly technical ones alongside the everyday ones.

As with other prefixes, the spelling alone doesn't prove the meaning. Words such as press, pretty and prey start with P-R-E without any sense of “before”. The observations on this page count how many entries leave another word behind when the three letters are removed; that is a spelling test, not a history lesson, but it is a useful guide for players who want to know how often a P, R and E can be stuck onto the front of an existing word.

Players also meet pre- inside longer words, where the same three letters do no prefix work at all, so treat the counts as patterns of spelling rather than of meaning.

The prefix dis generally marks an opposite, an absence or a removal. Compare agree and disagree, honest and dishonest, arm and disarm. Most dis- words came into English through Latin or French, and many of them were formed in those languages rather than in English, which is why some of them have no matching English base word: distract and dismal, for instance, don't break neatly into dis- plus a modern word.

On this page every word starting with D-I-S is counted, prefix or not, and the observations show how many still spell a word once those three letters are taken away. Expect a mix of clean pairs and coincidences. For word puzzles, dis- is worth remembering as a way to reach seven or eight letters from a four- or five-letter base, and the S in the middle means that a single S on your rack can sometimes be used inside the prefix rather than as a plural.

The prefix mis means “wrongly” or “badly”: to misspell is to spell something wrongly, to misread is to read it wrongly, and a mistrial is a trial that went wrong. Unlike un- and dis-, mis- rarely means a simple opposite; it describes doing the same thing, just poorly.

That makes mis- one of the more predictable prefixes. Many verbs accept it, and the resulting words keep the spelling of the base word intact, so the base usually survives when the three letters are removed. When a word such as misspell has a double S, that is simply the prefix's S meeting a base word that also starts with S. Words like mist and miser are reminders that the spelling alone isn't enough: they start with M-I-S but have nothing to do with the prefix.

The statistics below are computed from the open ENABLE word list, so they describe that list rather than English as a whole.

The prefix non means “not” and is the most neutral of the negative prefixes. Where un- can suggest something undone and dis- something reversed, non- usually just says a quality is absent: nonstop, nonfiction, nonsense. It is especially common in technical and formal vocabulary, and it is often written with a hyphen in everyday writing.

Word lists such as ENABLE contain only single unbroken words, so hyphenated forms do not appear, but many non- words that are commonly written solid are included. That gives this list an unusual shape: it holds a large share of long words, because non- tends to attach to words that are already long. The longest entries on this page show that clearly.

For puzzles, remember that N-O-N can also begin words that have no prefix, and that the double N appears when the base word itself starts with N, as in nonnative. Whether a given non- word is accepted in a game depends entirely on that game's dictionary.

The prefix out has two common meanings. The first is “outside” or “away”, as in outdoors, outlet and outpost. The second, very productive in English, is “do more or better than”: to outrun someone is to run faster than them, and to outlast them is to last longer. That second sense can attach to almost any verb of action, which is why word lists contain long runs of out- verbs, many of them rare in ordinary writing.

For word games, out- words are interesting because they are usually built from short, common base words, and the three prefix letters O, U and T are themselves common tiles. When a base word is already on the board, adding out- in front can be a cheap way to make a long play, if your game's dictionary has the longer word.

As always, not every word beginning O-U-T contains the prefix: outrage developed separately, even though it looks like out- plus rage.

The prefix over usually means “too much” (overcook, overpay, overdue) or “above, across” (overhead, overpass). Like out-, it is one of English's most productive prefixes, and it combines freely with verbs, adjectives and nouns, so long over- words are plentiful.

Because the prefix is four letters long and the base words tend to be ordinary, over- words are a good illustration of how word length in a list is driven by prefixes and suffixes as much as by roots. Many of the longest words on this page are an over- prefix on an already long base. A word game player is unlikely to hold every letter needed for those, but shorter forms such as overt, overdo and overlap show up regularly.

Note that overt starts with the same four letters without being an over- word in meaning; the counts here are about spelling only.

The prefix sub comes from Latin and means “under” or “below” (subway, submarine), and by extension “secondary” or “smaller part of” (subset, subplot). It is common in scientific and technical vocabulary, where it labels categories inside categories, so lists of sub- words lean toward the formal.

In older borrowings the B sometimes changed to match the next letter, which is why related Latin words begin with suc-, suf-, sug-, sup- or sus- instead; those words are not counted here, because this page is about the spelling S-U-B only. Plenty of other words start with these letters with no prefix at all, such as subtle in its modern sense and suburb in everyday use, so read the counts as a spelling pattern.

For players, sub- is a three-letter front hook worth knowing for a handful of everyday bases. Other everyday examples include subtotal and subway, where the meaning of the parts is still easy to see.

The prefix anti means “against” or “opposite to”: antiwar, antifreeze, antibody. It comes from Greek, and English uses it freely to build new words, many of them in science, medicine and politics. Like non-, it is often written with a hyphen in everyday writing, but this page counts only words that the ENABLE list spells solid.

A few words start with A-N-T-I without containing the prefix in its “against” sense. antic and antique are examples, and some words that begin ante mean “before”, a different prefix with a similar spelling. The “still form a word” count below is a spelling check and will include some of these coincidences.

Because anti- is four letters with only two vowels, anti- words tend to be long and consonant-rich. They rarely matter in everyday tile play, but they are useful for crossword-style puzzles where the length and a few crossing letters are known.

The ending ing is the most familiar suffix in English. It forms the present participle of verbs (“she is reading”) and the gerund, the verb used as a noun (“reading is fun”). It also appears in plain nouns that have drifted away from their verbs, such as building and ceiling, and in many words where -ing is not a suffix at all, like king, sing and thing.

Spelling rules around -ing explain many of the patterns in this list: a silent E is usually dropped (make becomes making), a final consonant is often doubled after a short vowel (run becomes running), and verbs ending in -ie switch to -y (tie becomes tying). Because so many verbs take -ing, the list of words ending in I-N-G is very long and is split here by the letter that comes before it.

The share of the whole list that ends in -ing shows how strongly inflected forms shape any word list.

The ending ed marks the past tense and past participle of regular verbs: walk, walked. It also forms adjectives from nouns, describing something that has a feature, as in bearded or talented. Irregular verbs such as go, see and take don't use it, which is why some common verbs are missing from this list.

The same spelling rules that shape -ing shape -ed: a final silent E merges with the ending (bake, baked), a final consonant after a short vowel is often doubled (stop, stopped), and a consonant plus Y becomes -ied (try, tried). Because nearly every regular verb has an -ed form, words ending in E-D make up a large slice of the word list, and the list is split here by the letter before E-D.

Some words end in these letters with no past-tense meaning at all, such as bed, red and seed; the counts include them.

The ending ly most often turns an adjective into an adverb: quick becomes quickly, calm becomes calmly. It can also make adjectives from nouns, describing something “like” or “happening every”, as in friendly, costly and weekly. Many -ly words therefore come in families, with the base word sitting next to the longer form in the list.

Spelling changes are fewer than with -ing or -ed, but a few are regular: adjectives ending in a consonant plus Y change Y to I (happy, happily), and those ending in -le often become -ly by dropping the E (gentle, gently). Words such as fly, holy and ugly end in L-Y without being formed with the suffix.

Because the base word survives in most -ly words, the “leave another word” count below is high, which is a handy reminder for word puzzles: if you can see an adjective, an adverb is often two letters away.

The ending er has two main grammatical jobs. On verbs it names the person or thing that does the action: a baker bakes, a reader reads, an opener opens. On short adjectives it forms the comparative: tall, taller; quick, quicker. On top of that, a great many plain words simply end in these two letters, such as water, mother and never.

That mix makes words ending in E-R one of the largest two-letter endings in the list, so the page is split by the letter that comes before. Spelling rules again leave fingerprints: doubled consonants (big, bigger), dropped silent E (write, writer) and Y turning into I (happy, happier).

For players, an E and an R are two of the most useful tiles to keep together, because so many words can be extended with them.

The ending est forms the superlative of short adjectives, the “most” form: tall, tallest; kind, kindest. Longer adjectives usually use “most” instead (“most beautiful”), which is why superlatives in a word list cluster around short, common base words.

The spelling rules match the comparative -er: double the final consonant after a short vowel (hot, hottest), drop a silent E (wide, widest) and change a final Y after a consonant to I (busy, busiest). In older English, -est was also a verb ending used with “thou”, and some of those forms survive in word lists.

Not every word ending in E-S-T is a superlative: nest, chest, forest and interest are ordinary nouns. The counts on this page include them, and the “leave another word” figure shows how often removing the three letters gives back a base word.

The suffix ness turns an adjective into a noun meaning “the state or quality of being”: kind, kindness; dark, darkness; aware, awareness. It is one of the most dependable suffixes in English: it is still used to make new words, it almost never changes the spelling of the base, and the meaning is easy to predict.

The one regular spelling change is the familiar Y to I after a consonant (happy, happiness). Because the base word nearly always survives intact, a very high share of the words on this page leave another word in the list when the four letters are removed, which you can check in the observations below.

Word lists also include plural forms such as kindnesses, which end in -nesses rather than -ness and so appear on other ending pages. For tile games, -ness is a long tail to hang on an adjective already on the board, where your game's dictionary allows it.

The suffix ful usually makes adjectives meaning “full of” or “having”: hopeful, careful, joyful. It also makes nouns of measurement, the amount that fills something: a spoonful, a handful, a cupful. Note the single L: the suffix is spelled with one L even though the word “full” has two.

Spelling changes are rare. A final Y after a consonant becomes I, as in beauty and beautiful, and otherwise the base usually stays as it is. That keeps the “leave another word” count on this page high.

The plural of a measurement noun is usually formed by adding S at the end (spoonfuls), and the older form with the S in the middle also exists in some word lists; check this list's entries before relying on either. Adverbs formed from -ful adjectives end in -fully and are counted on other pages, since they end in different letters.

The suffix less means “without”: careless, hopeless, endless. It is the natural partner of -ful, and many base words take both, giving pairs like careful and careless. Like -ness, it is still freely used to coin new words, and it usually leaves the base word's spelling untouched.

That regularity shows up in the numbers: a large share of the words on this page remain a word when the last four letters are removed. The exceptions are mostly words where L-E-S-S is not a suffix at all, such as bless and unless.

Adverbs and nouns built on -less words, such as carelessly and carelessness, end in other letters and appear on other ending pages. In word games, -less can turn a short noun into a long adjective with four common letters, two of them S, so it is worth checking when you hold a pair of S tiles.

The ending tion forms nouns of action or result, mostly from verbs of Latin origin: create, creation; inform, information; reduce, reduction. Strictly speaking the suffix is often -ion added to a stem that ends in T, but in spelling terms the four letters T-I-O-N are what you see, and that is what this page counts.

Because the verb and the noun often differ by more than just the ending (an E drops, a C becomes a T, or extra letters appear, as in explain and explanation), the “leave another word” count is lower here than for suffixes like -ness. Most -tion words are long and formal, and this is one of the endings where the longest entries in the list are found.

The pronunciation is the same “shun” sound as in -sion and -cian words, which end in different letters and are not included on this page.

The suffix able makes adjectives meaning “can be” or “worth being”: readable, washable, enjoyable. It is still productive, so new -able words appear regularly, and many of them are perfectly regular formations from verbs.

A few spelling rules apply. A silent E is often dropped (love, lovable), though it is kept after a soft C or G to keep the sound (change, changeable). Some words use the related ending -ible instead (visible, possible); those end in different letters and are not counted here. There is no simple rule for which ending a word takes, which is why both appear in spelling tests.

Several common words end in A-B-L-E without being formed with the suffix, such as table, cable and able itself. The figures below count every word in the list that ends with these four letters. Adverbs built on these adjectives end in -ably, as in comfortably, and appear on other pages.

The suffix ment turns verbs into nouns that name an action, its result or the means of doing it: develop, development; pay, payment; equip, equipment. Many of these nouns came into English from French, where the ending was already common.

The base verb usually keeps its spelling, including a silent E (move, movement), with a few well-known exceptions such as judgment in American spelling and argument, where the E of argue drops. That is why the share of words here that leave another word when the four letters are removed is fairly high, but not complete.

Words like cement, moment and comment end in M-E-N-T without a verb inside them that means the same thing. The page counts them all, so the numbers describe spelling patterns in the list rather than word history. Plural forms such as payments end in -ments and are counted on other ending pages.

The suffix ous forms adjectives meaning “full of” or “having the quality of”: danger, dangerous; fame, famous; joy, joyous. It came into English through French from Latin, and a large share of -ous words were borrowed whole rather than built in English, so many of them have no matching English base word.

That is why the “leave another word” figure on this page is much lower than for -ness or -less. Related endings such as -ious and -eous (various, gorgeous) still end in O-U-S and are counted here, which is one reason the list is longer than you might guess.

For word games, the vowel pair O and U makes -ous a handy way to use those two letters together at the end of a long word, and the letter before it is shown below, since it varies more than you might expect.

The suffix ish has several related meanings. On adjectives and nouns it means “somewhat” or “like”: reddish, childish, bookish. It also forms words for nationalities and languages, which are capitalized in ordinary writing and so mostly absent from a lowercase word list like ENABLE. In casual speech it has become a word on its own, but that use is too new for most word lists.

Some common words end in I-S-H without carrying the suffix, such as fish, dish, wish and finish, and many verbs from French end this way too (polish, publish, vanish), where it is part of the verb rather than a suffix with its own meaning.

The statistics below count every word in the list that ends with these three letters, and the observations show how many leave a word when the ending is removed, a quick way to see how often -ish is a true suffix.
